text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will join Israeli-Palestinian negotiations on Monday to try to close a deal on a long-delayed pullback from the West Bank town of Hebron, officials for both sides said.
"The Palestinian delegation led by (chief PLO negotiatior) Mahmoud Abbas and the Israeli team as well as the Americans will meet with Netanyahu at 2:30 p.m. (1230 GMT)," a senior PLO official said.

Palestinian officials reported unexpected progress on Monday in talks on Israel's long-delayed pullback from the West Bank town and said a U.S. mission was focused on closing a deal in time for Christmas.
They said some issues were left to be resolved in a meeting yet to be arranged between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Netanyahu.
"Both delegations have orders to finalise an accord tonight and if there is agreement, there could be a Netanyahu-Arafat meeting tonight," the PLO official said.
Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan told Reuters: "I know that the prime minister is supposed to meet with the negotiating teams.

"If progress is sufficient, then I presume that there will be a meeting between Netanyahu and Arafat. Whether or not it will be today or in the next couple of days remains to be seen," Bar-Illan said.

Israel and the PLO have accused each other of foot-dragging in more than three months of talks on Hebron, 80 percent of which was due to have been handed over to Arafat's Palestinian Authority months ago.

Netanyahu, who came to power in June vowing to take a tough line on Israeli security, has demanded protection for 400 Jewish militants in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs, a longtime flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews.

"If the Israeli side accepts and the committees finish their work today, this will open the door to a meeting between President Arafat and Netanyahu to resolve the remaining problems," Arafat's spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah said.
U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross flew to Cairo to brief Egypt on progress made in two days of Israeli-PLO talks.
Jibril Rajoub, head of Palestinian Preventive Security in the West Bank, said when asked if a deal could be clinched on Monday: "I hope so."

The U.S. envoy arrived in the Middle East on Saturday saying he hoped to re-energise talks. But he had played down hopes of a breakthrough, saying only that he expected to report to President Bill Clinton after a couple of days.
Only last week Arafat was questioning Ross's objectivity. But after meeting Ross for a second time in two days, Arafat expressed his thanks for the American's support.
"The two teams and the Americans, led by Ross, met with Arafat until dawn and we can finally say there was progress," said a PLO official who declined to be identified.
